lesson.title: Feeding the GPUs: Networking for AI Training
lesson.summary: AI training workloads demand a different kind of network than ordinary web traffic: massive, synchronized transfers between accelerators that must complete in microseconds, or the most expensive hardware in the building sits idle.
lesson.body:
Training a large neural network is not one computer doing one long computation. It is dozens, hundreds, or thousands of GPUs, spread across many servers, working on the same model at once. After each batch of data, every GPU has computed a slightly different update to the model's parameters, called a gradient, and before anyone can move to the next batch, those gradients have to be combined across all the GPUs so everyone ends up with the same updated model. This combining step, often implemented as an operation called all-reduce, means every GPU is sending and receiving data to and from every other GPU, all at once, many times per second, for the entire duration of training.

This pattern is almost the opposite of the traffic you have thought about so far in this course. A typical web server handles many independent, bursty requests that do not depend on each other. A training cluster instead needs a huge, synchronized, all to all exchange to finish before any GPU can do useful work again. If the network is slow, GPUs are not just waiting, they are burning electricity and depreciating on a lease while doing nothing. Consider training a large model across 512 GPUs: a single round of gradient synchronization can move tens of gigabytes across the cluster, and that round repeats thousands of times over a training run. Add even a few hundred microseconds of unnecessary latency to each round, and multiplied across a long training job, it becomes real wall clock time, and real money, since GPU time is billed by the hour.

This is where the low latency networking ideas from earlier in the course get pushed to an extreme. General purpose networking usually optimizes for throughput and fairness among many flows. AI cluster networking optimizes for finishing one enormous synchronized transfer as fast as possible, over and over. One key tool is RDMA, remote direct memory access, which lets a GPU on one server write directly into the memory of a GPU on another server without routing the data through the operating system's normal networking stack or burning CPU cycles copying it along the way. RDMA is typically delivered either over InfiniBand, a specialized networking technology built for this kind of cluster, or over ordinary Ethernet using RoCE, RDMA over Converged Ethernet, which brings similar direct memory access benefits to more standard hardware.

Topology matters just as much as the transport protocol. Data center network designers building AI clusters often use rail optimized, fat tree style topologies, where every GPU has close to full bandwidth available to every other GPU, and the network is deliberately not oversubscribed the way a typical enterprise network might be. In a rail optimized design, the network interface cards with the same number on every server are wired together onto a dedicated set of switches, so traffic patterns stay predictable and congestion in one part of the fabric does not spill over into unrelated traffic.

Because RDMA traffic is sensitive to dropped packets in a way that ordinary TCP traffic tolerates more gracefully, AI cluster networks frequently use lossless Ethernet features like priority flow control, plus congestion control schemes tuned specifically for this environment, to keep queues from overflowing and packets from being dropped under the huge synchronized bursts that all reduce operations create. None of this replaces the fundamentals you already know about how networks forward packets and why latency accumulates hop by hop. It applies those fundamentals under much stricter constraints, with specialized hardware and topology decisions built around one specific, extremely demanding traffic pattern: keeping expensive accelerators fed instead of waiting.
